articles.title: USD/JPY flirts with danger again as the 160.00 mark puts Japan intervention risks back in focus
articles.description: How many times can you poke the bear before it finally wakes up and bites? Well, dollar bulls appear to be keen on finding that out as USD/JPY starts to push toward the 160.00 level this week. The dollar continues to hold its own even amid a broader improvement in risk sentiment, while elevated Treasury yields are hardly doing the yen any favours. But at these levels, I'd argue that getting the direction right is only half the battle. Looking at the daily chart, buyers have already been turned away around the 160.00 level on a few occasions earlier this month, much like what we saw towards the start of September. For now, the convergence of the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages around 158.75-90 provides a useful technical reference point. Holding above that region keeps buyers in the hunt, whereas a sustained break below both levels could quickly put sellers back in the driver's seat. As for the upside potential, Goldman Sachs is essentially telling traders not to push their luck. The firm believes Japan's MOF remains willing to intervene again, especially if USD/JPY buyers keep testing the limits above the 160.00 mark: "We continue to believe that the MOF would intervene again if it deemed necessary, and the likelihood should increase as USD/JPY moves above 160 based on prior actions this year. That should keep yen vol low while broader USD pressures remain positive, as we expect investors to be reluctant to push USD/JPY to new highs, given the risk of intervention and recent signs of constructive shifts in other key domestic policies (e.g. monetary policy) that have tilted the asymmetry clearly towards a stronger yen." The firm's trade preference is rather telling too, with Goldman Sachs continuing to favour shorting EUR/JPY instead. That allows for maintaining exposure to a stronger yen without directly betting against the dollar. As such, it also offers some protection against dollar-positive developments involving energy prices, bond yields and broader risk sentiment. So, what would we be watching from here? Besides the obvious technical hurdles, pay close attention to the speed at which USD/JPY advances and any escalation in verbal warnings from Tokyo. The 160.00 mark isn't necessarily a hard line for intervention but any quick and sudden moves beyond that could invite a rather different response from Japanese officials. articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the roof. At least, I assume it was a pet. I can’t think of any other reason that doesn’t sound considerably more sinister. Continue reading...
